cards.front: An infant's normal bicarbonate sits a few mmol/L below the adult range — around [___] mmol/L — because the renal bicarbonate threshold is lower.
cards.context:
The infant kidney has a lower renal bicarbonate threshold, so it spills bicarbonate at a plasma level an adult would retain. The steady-state bicarbonate therefore sits a few mmol/L lower.

The consequence is a normal infant looking mildly acidotic against adult reference values, and a genuinely acidotic infant looking worse than the numbers suggest.

It also explains why infants have so little buffering reserve and decompensate quickly in gastroenteritis, sepsis or a metabolic crisis.

cards.front: An anterior diaphragmatic hernia through the foramen of [___] presents later than the posterolateral type.
cards.context:
The other named defect, and the one that presents outside the newborn period.

A Morgagni hernia is anterior. On the film it is a centrally placed gas-filled structure overlying the heart and extending to both sides of the chest, and a contrast study down the nasogastric tube confirms it.

cards.front: Hand hygiene when hands are [___] should use alcohol-based hand rub rather than soap and water.
cards.context:
Alcohol-based hand rub is first-line for visibly clean hands: faster, better tolerated, and more effective against most organisms.

The exceptions are the ones alcohol does not kill.

cards.front: [___] velocity is more clinically useful than a single height measurement; crossing 2 centile lines warrants investigation regardless of current percentile.
cards.context:
A single height plotted on a growth chart shows where the child sits vs peers but says little about change.

Crossing 2+ major centile lines (downward = slowing, upward = accelerated) warrants investigation.

Plot serial measurements — frequency 6-monthly under 2y, annually thereafter.

cards.front: Perthes disease: idiopathic AVN of femoral head in boys aged [___]; younger age at onset = better prognosis.
cards.context:
Perthes (Legg-Calve-Perthes) is idiopathic AVN of the femoral head in boys aged 4-10y. Blood supply interruption causes head fragmentation and collapse, then revascularisation and remodelling.

Presents with progressive hip pain, limp and a positive Trendelenburg sign. Younger onset = better prognosis because there is more remodelling time.

Long-term outcome depends on residual femoral-head deformity and joint congruence; only a minority require total hip arthroplasty by midlife.

cards.front: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes 95% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH); autosomal recessive; newborn screen detects elevated [___].
cards.context:
21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for ~95% of CAH cases. Autosomal recessive.

The enzyme block prevents cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, shunting precursors to androgens (causing virilisation in females, salt-wasting from aldosterone deficiency).

cards.front: A septic neonate with seizures, vesicles or hepatitis needs empiric [___] added while HSV is investigated.
cards.context:
HSV can mimic bacterial sepsis and waiting for a classic vesicular rash misses cases. Maternal or recent HSV exposure, seizures or abnormal neurology, vesicles, keratitis and hepatitis all lower the treatment threshold.

Add empiric aciclovir while testing when the presentation suggests HSV; do not replace the bacterial regimen with antiviral monotherapy.

cards.front: Gastro-oesophageal reflux (GOR) is physiological in infants — peaks at [___] months and resolves by 12-18 months as the lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) matures. Distinguish from GORD (= GOR with complications).
cards.context:
Physiological GOR (gastro-oesophageal reflux) is the 'happy spitter' — frequent regurgitation but normal weight gain, no distress, no respiratory issues. Common in infants because the LES tone is immature.

Peaks ~4 months, resolves by 12-18 months as the LES matures. Pathological GORD = reflux causing complications (FTT, oesophagitis, aspiration).

cards.front: Neuroblastoma most commonly arises in the [___] medulla.
cards.context: Neuroblastoma arises from sympathetic neural-crest tissue. The adrenal medulla is the most common primary site (~40%); abdominal/paraspinal chain sites follow. Crosses the midline; raccoon-eye metastases are classic.

cards.front: The most common type of tracheo-oesophageal fistula is [___] (proximal atresia with distal fistula), accounting for ~85% of cases.
cards.context:
Type C (proximal atresia + distal fistula) accounts for 85% of cases. The clinical clue is a newborn who drools excessively and chokes on first feed.

On chest X-ray (CXR), an orogastric tube coils in the upper pouch. Gas in the stomach confirms a distal fistula; absent abdominal gas suggests pure atresia.

cards.front: Absence of [___] by 12 months is a key early red flag for autism spectrum disorder.
cards.context:
Pointing is a joint-attention behaviour — child uses the gesture to draw a caregiver's attention to a shared object (proto-declarative pointing).

It's more specific than language delay because language can lag for many reasons; joint attention deficits are a core autism signal.

Absent pointing, poor eye contact, no social smiling, or no response to name by 12 months should trigger early intervention referral. Intervention in the first 2-3 years has the largest effect.

cards.front: In post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), the complement pattern is low [___] with normal C4 (alternative pathway activation).
cards.context:
The complement pattern is a useful discriminator in paediatric nephritis. PSGN activates the alternative complement pathway, so C3 is consumed while C4 stays normal.

That pattern separates PSGN from lupus nephritis, where both C3 and C4 are usually low. C3 should recover within 6-8 weeks; persistent hypocomplementaemia suggests another diagnosis and needs nephrology review.

cards.front: A single low weight cannot establish growth faltering; assessment needs [___] measurements on a growth chart.
cards.context: Direction over time distinguishes a steady small child from one falling away from their previous growth pattern.

cards.front: A 2-year-old had a witnessed choking episode on peanuts and now has a focal right-sided wheeze; the inspiratory CXR is normal. Even with a normal film, the next step is [___].
cards.context:
Most inhaled foreign bodies are radiolucent, so a normal inspiratory film excludes nothing. A witnessed choking episode with a new focal wheeze is the diagnosis on history alone.

Rigid bronchoscopy under anaesthesia both confirms and removes the object. Waiting for pneumonia to declare it is the failure mode.

cards.front: For likely methicillin-susceptible S. aureus, prefer an anti-staphylococcal [___] over routine vancomycin.
cards.context:
For methicillin-susceptible staphylococcal infection, an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam such as flucloxacillin or cefazolin is narrower and usually preferred.

Vancomycin or another MRSA-active agent is reserved for a genuine MRSA risk, severe beta-lactam hypersensitivity or a syndrome-specific indication, then reviewed when microbiology returns.

cards.front: A newborn with no anal opening and failure to pass meconium has an [___].
cards.context:
Inspect the newborn perineum to confirm a normally positioned anal opening. Stool can pass through an abnormal fistula, so stool passage does not exclude a malformation.

An absent anus or abnormal outlet needs prompt neonatal surgical assessment. Delay risks bowel obstruction; associated urinary, spinal and cardiac anomalies also need assessment.

cards.front: Most common bacterial cause of paediatric tonsillitis is Group A Streptococcus, peak 5-15 years, rare under [___]; treat with phenoxymethylpenicillin to prevent rheumatic fever.
cards.context:
GABHS (S. pyogenes) is the dominant bacterial cause of paediatric tonsillitis — peak 5-15y, rare <3y (immature lymphoid tissue, different flora). Most sore throats in young children are viral.

GABHS needs phenoxymethylpenicillin 10 days, mainly to prevent acute rheumatic fever (antibiotics do NOT prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).

Tonsillectomy for recurrent cases meeting Paradise criteria (7+/yr, 5/yr for 2y, 3/yr for 3y).

cards.front: An undescended testis rarely descends after 3 months of age — refer then, aiming for orchidopexy at [___] months.
cards.context:
Most testes that will descend do so in the first few months of life; beyond that, waiting adds nothing, so refer rather than watch.

Early surgery protects heat-sensitive germ cells — the longer a testis sits inguinal, the worse the fertility outcome. Prepubertal orchidopexy also lowers (never removes) malignancy risk and keeps the testis examinable.

cards.front: Short stature = height <[___]rd centile for age and gender; commonest causes are constitutional delay and familial short stature.
cards.context:
Short stature = height <3rd percentile for age and gender.

Pathological causes (GH deficiency, hypothyroidism, coeliac, chronic illness, Turner syndrome) are less common but require workup if growth velocity is poor.

cards.front: Burn first aid uses cool running water at roughly 15°C, never [___], which causes vasoconstriction and deepens the burn.
cards.context:
Cool running water relieves pain and limits tissue injury; colder is not necessarily better. Ice can impair blood flow to injured tissue and worsen damage.

Cool the affected area while keeping the rest of the child warm. Monitor for hypothermia, especially when cooling a large area.

cards.front: Scarlet fever (Group A Strep, toxin-mediated rash) needs phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days; this prevents [___] fever but NOT post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
cards.context:
Scarlet fever is the toxin-mediated rash variant of GAS pharyngitis — pyrogenic exotoxins drive the sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, and Pastia's lines.

Antibiotics prevent acute rheumatic fever (cross-reactive autoimmunity vs heart, joints, brain, at 2-4 weeks) but do NOT reliably prevent PSGN.

PSGN is immune-complex nephritis (haematuria + hypertension, at 1-2 weeks); treating the index infection neither averts it nor treats it once established. Complete the full 10-day course to eradicate the organism.

cards.front: The main determinant of survival in congenital diaphragmatic hernia is the degree of [___], not the hernia itself.
cards.context:
Abdominal contents in the chest compress the developing lung throughout the second and third trimesters, so by birth the ipsilateral lung has too few alveoli and abnormal pulmonary vasculature.

This is why fixing the hernia surgically does not rescue a baby — there simply isn't enough functional lung.

cards.front: Isotretinoin is highly effective for severe acne but is teratogenic — requires two forms of contraception in females; also monitor [___], lipids, and mood.
cards.context:
Isotretinoin is the most effective severe-acne treatment but is highly teratogenic (craniofacial, cardiac, CNS, thymic anomalies).

Also monitor LFTs, fasting lipids, and mood (possible suicidality link). Avoid alcohol, tetracyclines (additive ICP risk), and waxing (skin fragility). Standard course is 4-6 months to cumulative ~120-150 mg/kg.

cards.front: In a well newborn with erythema toxicum, the cells typically abundant in a pustule smear are [___].
cards.context: This benign eruption resolves spontaneously. A pustular rash in an unwell newborn needs urgent assessment for infection rather than reassurance.

cards.front: An avulsed permanent tooth should be [___] immediately, or stored in milk, to save it.
cards.context:
Time-critical for PERMANENT teeth: reimplant immediately (or store in milk / saliva) and seek dental care — survival falls fast with dry time.

Tap water is a poor hypotonic medium, but is preferable to air-drying if no better medium is available. Avulsed PRIMARY (baby) teeth are NOT reimplanted (risk to the developing permanent tooth).

cards.front: A ventilated preterm infant with hyaline membrane disease acutely desaturates; an etched heart border indicates [___], for which positive-pressure ventilation is an important risk factor.
cards.context:
This is a recognition-under-pressure card: the sign is subtle and the situation is time-critical. Pleural air between heart and lung outlines the mediastinal border unusually crisply — the etched heart border.

In a ventilated preterm infant with hyaline membrane disease who suddenly desaturates, that over-sharp border is a pneumothorax until proven otherwise.

Positive-pressure ventilation is an important risk factor, but neonatal pneumothorax can also occur spontaneously or with underlying lung disease.

cards.front: DSM-5 requires that autism features be present from the early [___] period, even if recognised much later.
cards.context:
Candidates reliably recall the two symptom domains and lose the marks on when the features must have started.

They must date from the early developmental period, even if they only became obvious once social demands outgrew the child's capacity.

That is why a first presentation in high school still counts, provided the history reaches back.

cards.front: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn typically resolves within [___] hours.
cards.context:
The time course is the diagnosis. Transient tachypnoea is self-limiting, so distress that is still worsening beyond this window argues for sepsis, surfactant deficiency or a cardiac cause instead.

Waiting it out is only safe while the baby is improving.

cards.front: Thalassaemia produces microcytic anaemia with normal iron stores (because the defect is globin-chain production, not iron) and a [___] RDW (uniform small cells). The opposite pattern — depleted iron stores plus an elevated RDW (cells of mixed sizes during recovery) — points to iron deficiency.
cards.context:
Thalassaemia is autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy — reduced or absent production of α or β globin chains.

Distinguish from iron deficiency: low ferritin (depleted stores) + high RDW (anisocytosis from variable cell sizes during recovery).

cards.front: A well 3-year-old has a bulging tympanic membrane, an effusion and no discharge. The appropriate first step is analgesia plus [___] for 48 hours; the single feature in the history that would most clearly override this in an infant is age under 6 months.
cards.context:
Most uncomplicated acute otitis media is analgesia and 48 hours of watchful waiting. The examinable skill is who should NOT wait.

Age under 6 months, systemic illness, discharge, craniofacial anomaly, immunocompromise, a cochlear implant, and high-risk Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children all lower the threshold.

Bilateral disease under 2 is not by itself an automatic RCH indication — follow the local antimicrobial guideline.

cards.front: Dynamic supraglottic obstruction usually produces inspiratory stridor; vocal-cord or subglottic obstruction is often [___].
cards.context:
Respiratory phase is a localisation clue, not a one-to-one map. Dynamic supraglottic obstruction such as laryngomalacia usually causes inspiratory stridor. Vocal-cord or subglottic obstruction is often biphasic.

Tracheal obstruction may be predominantly expiratory, while a fixed obstruction anywhere in the laryngotracheal airway can be biphasic.

Expiratory stridor is an upper-airway sound and should not be equated with lower-airway wheeze.

cards.front: West syndrome triad: epileptic [___] (1-2 seconds, repetitive in clusters), hypsarrhythmia on EEG, developmental regression; treat with prednisolone or vigabatrin.
cards.context:
Hypsarrhythmia is a chaotic EEG background: large, irregular slow waves mixed with spikes from several regions. It is not a regular seizure rhythm.

Suspected infantile spasms need urgent awake/sleep EEG and neurology review; a normal early EEG does not exclude them. Prompt treatment reduces developmental harm.

Treatment is specialist-led: high-dose prednisolone is usual first-line therapy; vigabatrin is first-line for tuberous sclerosis. Other treatable causes need specific therapy.

cards.front: Waving bye-bye, putting a block into a cup and looking for a toy hidden under a blanket fit the NSW [___]-month profile.
cards.context:
The twelve-month profile adds communication and problem solving: waving, using a special name for a parent, putting an object into a container and looking for a visibly hidden toy.

Gross motor expectation is pulling to stand and furniture cruising—not a hard requirement to walk independently on the first birthday.

cards.front: An otherwise comfortable, thriving infant repeatedly spills small mouthfuls of milk after feeds. This pattern fits physiological [___].
cards.context: Reflux becomes disease when it causes troublesome feeding, growth or respiratory symptoms. Forceful or green vomiting needs assessment for another cause.

cards.front: With the first breaths after birth, pulmonary vascular resistance [___], allowing pulmonary blood flow to rise sharply.
cards.context:
Lung aeration and rising oxygen tension dilate the pulmonary vessels; PVR falls and left-sided pressures rise, closing the foramen ovale flap.

This transition is why duct-dependent lesions can look well at birth and collapse days later as the duct closes.

cards.front: Haemoglobin is at its lifetime peak at birth — about [___] g/L in a term baby — and then falls to a physiological trough of roughly 100 g/L.
cards.context:
The newborn arrives polycythaemic because the fetus grows in a low-oxygen environment and compensates with a high red-cell mass.

That mass is then dismantled: fetal red cells are short-lived, and the sudden rise in arterial oxygen at birth removes the stimulus to make more.

The result is a fall of roughly half over the first two months, which is why the newborn value and the infant value look like they belong to different patients.

cards.front: Persistent middle-ear fluid without acute infection — the commonest cause of childhood conductive hearing loss — is otitis media with [___].
cards.context:
Fluid persists in the middle ear after the acute infection settles, with no signs of acute inflammation.

It's the commonest cause of conductive hearing loss in children and can delay speech — most resolve spontaneously over weeks to months.

cards.front: A confidential consult follows when a 15-year-old understands her sexual-health decision, asks that her parents not be told, and there is no [___] concern.
cards.context: A young person who understands a health decision can consent to it, and the consult stays confidential. Confidentiality yields for a safeguarding risk, not because a parent wants to be told.

reference.title: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

cards.front: Portal hypertension in chronic paediatric liver disease usually results from intrahepatic [___] raising resistance to portal blood flow.
cards.context:
Portal hypertension is raised pressure in the portal venous system.

In chronic paediatric liver disease the resistance is usually intrahepatic — fibrosis and cirrhosis from any cause — though post-hepatic obstruction as in Budd-Chiari syndrome can produce the same downstream picture.

Inherited causes such as Wilson disease and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency can reach this stage; this section is about managing the portal pressure and its consequences, not diagnosing the underlying disease.

cards.front: Paediatric CXR hyperinflation: visibility of more than [___] posterior ribs above the diaphragm; indicates small airway air trapping.
cards.context:
Air trapped behind narrowed small airways flattens the diaphragms and pushes them caudally — counting how many posterior ribs are visible above each hemidiaphragm gives a quick estimate of hyperinflation.

In a wheezy child this supports bronchiolitis or asthma. In a toddler with sudden-onset unilateral wheeze, asymmetric hyperinflation should prompt consideration of an inhaled foreign body.

cards.front: The Australian Asthma Handbook assigns no chronic asthma severity grade; ongoing asthma is instead classified by level of recent symptom [___].
cards.context:
Students hunt the Australian Asthma Handbook for severity grades and find none, because AAH does not assign them.

AAH frames ongoing asthma by recent symptom control and by the treatment step needed to hold it. Severity, where used at all, is a retrospective judgement.

The mild/moderate/severe persistent tiers are older US NAEPP and legacy GINA language. In Australia they survive mainly in PBS indication wording.

cards.front: Paediatric inguinal hernias are almost always [___] (patent processus vaginalis) and require prompt surgical repair due to high incarceration risk (~30% in the first year).
cards.context:
The embryological mechanism is failure of the processus vaginalis to close after testicular descent — bowel then follows the same path through the internal ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

This anatomy also explains why watchful waiting is wrong here: the patent processus is a fixed structural defect that won't heal, and incarceration risk is ~30% in the first year of life.

cards.front: For children under four, GCS motor 6 includes [___] movement or obeying verbal commands.
cards.context:
Motor under four differs subtly from age four and over. Score 6 includes spontaneous movement or obeying verbal commands (not 'obeys commands' alone as the only route to 6).

Score 5 is localising to pain or withdrawing to touch — touch withdrawal counts as 5, not 4.

These tweaks prevent under-scoring a moving infant who is not yet following commands reliably.

cards.front: Bruising in a non-mobile infant with posterior rib fractures requires a [___] and mandatory notification.
cards.context:
Both findings are inflicted-injury patterns. Pre-mobile infants don't bruise themselves; posterior rib fractures come from chest compression.

Skeletal survey documents the full burden — repeat at 11-14 days catches healing fractures.

Notify child protection. The team investigates; your role is to flag, not confirm abuse.

cards.front: A hypotonic newborn with upslanting fissures, a flat nasal bridge and a single palmar crease most likely has [___].
cards.context:
Neonatal hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat nasal bridge and a single palmar crease suggest trisomy 21.

The phenotype prompts diagnostic chromosomal testing and assessment for associated cardiac and gastrointestinal disease.

cards.front: The EpiPen Jr auto-injector, for a child 7.5-20 kg, delivers [___] mg of adrenaline.
cards.context: Auto-injectors are fixed-dose. The EpiPen Jr (0.15 mg) covers roughly 7.5-20 kg (about 1-5 years); below 7.5 kg a drawn-up dose is used instead.

cards.front: Kocher with [___] or more of fever >38.5, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40 and WCC >12 needs urgent joint aspiration, not NSAIDs.
cards.context:
The Kocher criteria are a bedside rule for the child with an acutely painful hip: septic arthritis (needs urgent washout) versus transient synovitis (settles with rest).

Four items: fever >38.5°C, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WCC >12.

Three or more predicts septic arthritis in about 93% of cases, so the joint is aspirated rather than watched; one item or none, it is probably irritable hip.

cards.front: Per the Australian Child Maltreatment Study, about 6 in 10 children experience maltreatment; the commonest single type is exposure to [___] violence; health professionals are mandatory reporters in all Australian jurisdictions.
cards.context:
The Australian Child Maltreatment Study (2023, n=8,503) found ~62% of children experience at least one of five maltreatment types.

By population prevalence the commonest is exposure to domestic violence (~40%); neglect is the LEAST common (~9%). The older 'neglect most common' figure came from notification data, not prevalence.

Health professionals are mandatory reporters in all states/territories. Threshold = REASONABLE concern: flag, don't investigate or prove abuse.

cards.front: Chronic transfusion in beta thalassaemia major causes [___] overload, treated with chelation.
cards.context: Lifelong transfusions cause iron overload (cardiac and hepatic toxicity). Treatment is iron chelation — deferasirox first-line, deferoxamine alternative.

cards.front: Neuroblastoma can arise anywhere along the sympathetic chain from neck to pelvis, but its single commonest primary site is the adrenal [___].
cards.context:
Neural-crest cells migrate to form the paraspinal ganglia and the core of the adrenal gland, so the tumour can appear anywhere from neck to pelvis — abdomen most often, posterior mediastinum next.

An adrenal primary sits above the kidney and displaces it downward on imaging, unlike Wilms' tumour, which arises within the renal parenchyma itself.

cards.front: Mastoiditis swelling is postero-superior to the pinna, pushing it down and [___]; needs IV antibiotics + grommet ± cortical mastoidectomy.
cards.context:
Acute mastoiditis is the most common suppurative complication of AOM — infection spreads from middle ear into mastoid air cells.

Other features: fever, progressive ear pain despite AOM antibiotics, discharge through perforated TM, conductive hearing loss. Mostly <3y, Strep pneumoniae; CT temporal bones confirms + identifies intracranial extension.

Treat with IV 3rd-gen ceph (ceftriaxone), grommet, cortical mastoidectomy if abscess — late presentation → meningitis, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, brain abscess.

cards.front: An infantile haemangioma threatens vision and needs systemic drug treatment. The usual first-line medicine is oral [___].
cards.context:
Most infantile haemangiomas need observation, but lesions threatening vision, breathing or function need specialist assessment. Propranolol reduces growth and promotes involution.

Treatment requires a prescribed plan and monitoring. Poor feeding increases the risk of hypoglycaemia.

cards.front: A barking, seal-like cough with inspiratory stridor in a 1–2 year old is [___].
cards.context: Recognise croup by the sound: a barking, seal-like cough with noisy inspiration (stridor) in a toddler. Most cases are parainfluenza and the diagnosis is clinical — no imaging needed.

cards.front: In children, Hepatitis A is self-limiting and never becomes a chronic carrier state, whereas Hepatitis B acquired at [___] carries a high (~90%) risk of becoming chronic.
cards.context:
This is the single discriminating fact for paediatrics. Hep A is an acute illness only — the child recovers fully and never becomes a chronic carrier (no chronic-liver-disease risk).

Hep B is the opposite when caught young: the younger the child at infection, the higher the chance it becomes chronic.

A baby infected at birth has roughly a 90% chance of chronic infection (versus <5% for an infected adult) — which is the whole reason the birth-dose vaccine matters.

cards.front: In post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), the complement pattern is low C3 with normal [___] (alternative pathway activation).
cards.context:
The complement pattern is a useful discriminator in paediatric nephritis. PSGN activates the alternative complement pathway, so C3 is consumed while C4 stays normal.

That pattern separates PSGN from lupus nephritis, where both C3 and C4 are usually low. C3 should recover within 6-8 weeks; persistent hypocomplementaemia suggests another diagnosis and needs nephrology review.

cards.front: Most common cause of croup is parainfluenza; peak age ~[___] years.
cards.context: Parainfluenza accounts for ~75% of croup. The peak age (1-2 years) reflects subglottic narrowness — same oedema in older children causes much less obstruction.

cards.front: Because valine is hydrophobic, on deoxygenation HbS molecules [___] into long rigid fibres that distort the red cell into the classic sickle shape, driving vaso-occlusion.
cards.context:
The exposed hydrophobic patch on deoxy-HbS binds a complementary pocket on an adjacent beta-chain, so fibres build only in the deoxygenated state and dissolve on re-oxygenation.

This is why crises are precipitated by hypoxia, dehydration, acidosis and infection, and why the defect is intermolecular (between molecules) rather than a problem with oxygen binding itself.

cards.front: Hyaline membrane disease is prevented with antenatal [___] given to the mother and treated with exogenous surfactant instilled via the endotracheal tube.
cards.context:
Treatment follows directly from the mechanism, and both halves are examinable.

Antenatal corticosteroids given to the mother accelerate fetal surfactant production. Exogenous surfactant is then instilled after birth down the endotracheal tube.

cards.front: Mild paediatric gastro dehydration: rehydrate with [___] (formulated for sodium-glucose co-transport); avoid high-sugar drinks (osmotic load worsens diarrhoea).
cards.context:
ORS (Hydralyte, Gastrolyte) maximises gut water absorption via the sodium-glucose co-transporter — glucose entering the enterocyte drags sodium, and water follows osmotically.

High-sugar fluids (juice, cordial, soft/sports drinks) do the opposite — excess glucose isn't matched by sodium, so the osmotic load pulls water INTO the lumen and worsens diarrhoea.

Plain water has no glucose to drive uptake at all; the fixed Na 60-90 / glucose 75-110 mmol/L ratio is engineered for this. Single-dose ondansetron before ORS reduces vomiting and improves oral rehydration success.
